appraisal_events.evidence: « Swann était trop fin pour ne pas voir que Mme de Guermantes cherchait en ce moment à "faire de l'esprit Guermantes" et sans grands frais, car elle ne faisait que resservir sous une forme moins parfaite d'anciens mots d'elle. » Her portrait of the princesse (« un peu idiote », « elle est nébuleuse, elle est Hesse-Darmstadt, Saint-Empire et gnan gnan », « une charmante loufoque ») is what is thus devalued.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator, through Swann's perception, exposes the duchesse's celebrated wit as a cheap, self-recycling performance, so her mocking sketch of the princesse registers as manufactured routine rather than as a genuine rhetorical triumph. The stance is endorsed: the narrator adds his own gêne and assimilates the surrounding insincerity to Legrandin's and his parents' hypocrisy.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Voyons, Oriane, qu'est-ce que vous dites... Marie bête ? Elle a tout lu, elle est musicienne comme le violon » ; then « Oriane, il faudrait au moins raconter la vérité et ne pas en manger la moitié », followed by his long rectification addressed to Swann and the jab « Mme de Guermantes, qui ne me fait pas souvent l'honneur de me consulter, a cru devoir aller mettre une carte dans la semaine à l'Élysée ». She had already tried to change the subject, « voyant que l'histoire de sa carte à Mme Carnot paraissait courroucer M. de Guermantes ».
appraisal_events.explanation: In front of Swann and the narrator the duc contradicts his wife, accuses her of telling a half-truth, and takes the anecdote away from her, pinning the social faux pas on her; she yields by attempting to change the subject. The narrator reports the correction deadpan rather than visibly endorsing it.

status_effects.explanation: Her command of the conversation collapses twice over: the narrator strips her wit of originality, and her husband then publicly corrects her version and seizes the narration while she retreats to another subject.
She comes off worse locally because the passage frames her esprit as second-hand and cheaply won, and her mockery of the princesse as a rehearsed effect.
He wins the local exchange: he rebuts her judgment of Marie, imposes his corrected account on the company, and she gives way — though his closing justification qualifies how much he really gains.

ambiguities: « le Président et sa femme » / « l'Élysée » here denote M. and Mme Carnot, who are named in the passage; the reference sheet's alias mapping of « le Président de la République » to M. Grevy does not apply, so the Carnots are listed with their verbatim surface forms as unresolved.

The narrator's stance toward the duc's rectification is layered: he plainly wins the point against Oriane, but his closing grounds for offence (M. Carnot being the grandson of a revolutionary judge who had « onze des nôtres » executed) invite ironic reading, which would blunt or reverse his local gain.
